A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Lawma and the same 260 legal annotation tasks. Their text, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching retained material across relocation and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original baseline evaluations, fine-tuning experiments, sample-efficiency studies, cross-court transfer results, and intercoder-agreement analyses.

after.justification: v2 reports original evaluations of updated models, prompting comparisons, fine-tuning results, and additional metric and class-balancing analyses in Appendix B.

M1.justification: The proposed Lawma family adopts different pretrained backbones: v1's principal models use Llama 3, whereas v2 uses Llama 3.1/3.2/3.3 and adds SmolLM2-based models. This updates the underlying models while retaining the same supervised multitask fine-tuning approach; no new loss or specialization mechanism is introduced.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same Supreme Court and Court of Appeals sources and the same 260 tasks. The complete task catalog in v1 Appendix B matches v2 Appendix D. Naming the collection CaselawQA, changing evaluation sample sizes, and testing alternative metrics do not add task or domain coverage.

E2.justification: The main comparisons expand to GPT-4o, GPT-4.5 Preview, Claude 3.7 Sonnet, o3-mini, DeepSeek R1, Qwen 2.5, and newer Llama models. Saul 7B is replaced by SaulLM 54B. The sample-efficiency reference changes from GPT-4 to Claude 3.7 Sonnet, while older GPT-4 and Llama 3 comparisons remain in Appendix B.

E3.justification: v2 introduces a 10,000-example main test set, sampled equally from the two court databases, and emphasizes per-example aggregate accuracy rather than v1's parallel case and task averages. It adopts chain-of-thought evaluation and adds 15-shot Llama comparisons, replacing the limited GPT-4 3-shot check. Model configurations change substantially; reported training volume increases from 1.96B to 2.2B tokens, and Lawma 70B training changes from one to three epochs. Appendix B adds alternative metrics and evaluation without majority-class subsampling.

E4.justification: v2 adds systematic prompting comparisons, metric and class-balancing sensitivity analyses, and a broader intercoder-agreement analysis. The earlier Pythia/Llama fine-tuning scaling curves and cross-court checkpoint trajectory are replaced by generalist-model scaling and a revised transfer comparison. The single-task specialization analysis is retained rather than newly added.

E5.justification: v1 explicitly identifies 90% Clopper-Pearson intervals and explains aggregation of task-level error bars. v2 retains visible benchmark error bars but omits those definitions and confidence-level explanations. Both versions retain five random seeds and 95% confidence intervals for sample-efficiency experiments; no increase in repeated runs is established.

E6.justification: v1 Table 1 reports GPT-4 mean task accuracy of 62.89%; v2 Figures 1 and 9 report 78% for Claude 3.7 Sonnet, 83% for Lawma 135M, and 88% for Lawma 70B under the revised evaluation. The sample-efficiency finding changes from matching GPT-4 on all ten highlighted tasks with 1,000 examples to matching Claude on seven, using an updated backbone. Appendix B adds results such as macro-F1 of 0.49 for GPT-4 and 0.65 for Lawma 8B. These are different-setting results, not direct performance gains over v1. The intercoder table and single-task specialization results are retained.

T1.justification: Neither version introduces formal theorems or proofs. The pretraining-compute approximation C approximately equals 6ND and the reasoning about adjusted accuracy and intercoder agreement are retained. The additional metric evaluations do not introduce new mathematical results.

C1.justification: The central claim broadens from an 8B fine-tuned model outperforming GPT-4 to models as small as 135M outperforming the evaluated contemporary commercial models. The abstract also revises the data-efficiency claim from tens to hundreds of examples to hundreds to a thousand. The introduction places greater emphasis on specialization for the precise target tasks.

C2.justification: v2 qualifies v1's optimistic discussion of transfer with an explicit warning that Lawma may not outperform commercial models outside its training databases. It also explains LegalBERT's poor performance through its small size and short context window and interprets the new prompting and scaling results. Existing cautions about imperfect accuracy and restriction to U.S. courts remain.

D1.justification: v2 adds dataset and test-set counts, reports LM Eval Harness availability, and specifies newer model snapshots and reasoning settings. Appendix C updates selected backbone and training details while retaining most optimizer, hardware, and compute disclosures. The original code, dataset, and model access statement remains; the retained Pythia/Llama 2 scaling instructions are not reconciled with the revised main experiments.

R1.justification: v2 adds discussion of earlier ideological-direction classifiers, open-source legal-model evaluations, and legal data in general pretraining, alongside references for newer models and the evaluation framework. Some older model and prompting references disappear. The basic positioning of task-specific specialization relative to general-purpose legal models remains intact.

P1.justification: The abstract and contribution narrative are substantially rewritten around legal annotation and CaselawQA. Evaluation methodology and baselines receive separate sections, generalization and single-task specialization are reordered, and highlighted-task descriptions move from the main text to Appendix A. These are substantial narrative and structural changes beyond additions of experimental content.

P2.justification: v2 replaces the opening per-task difference chart with an aggregate model comparison, substantially redesigns the main comparison displays, and adds prompting, scaling, intercoder, and appendix metric plots. The prompt example becomes a numbered figure. Conversely, v1 Figure 9 and Table 2 are retained as v2 Figure 13 and Table 1, and the task catalog mainly undergoes pagination changes.

improvement.justification: v1's central argument relied heavily on GPT-4 with direct prompting and a limited 3-shot check. v2's broader comparator set and chain-of-thought/15-shot controls substantially strengthen the evidence that specialization's advantage survives stronger prompting alternatives. Appendix B additionally tests dependence on metrics and class balancing. These gains outweigh reporting drawbacks: benchmark interval definitions are dropped, some training instructions are outdated, and scores occasionally conflict between prose and figures, such as 82% versus 83% for Lawma 135M.
